questions.stem: You are examining Adam, 74, in general practice for worsening breathlessness. On auscultation you hear a harsh ejection systolic murmur, loudest at the right 2nd intercostal space. Which next step best shows the examiner that this is aortic stenosis?
options: Roll him onto his left side and listen at the apex with the bell
Listen at the left lower sternal edge during deep inspiration
Listen over both carotids with the diaphragm while he holds his breath
Listen in the left axilla with the diaphragm in held expiration
questions.why: The aortic stenosis murmur radiates along the direction of flow into the carotids. Listen over the carotids with the patient holding his breath so breath sounds do not mask it.
notes: Left lateral position with the bell at the apex brings out the low-pitched diastolic rumble of mitral stenosis.
Louder in inspiration at the left lower sternal edge points to a right-sided lesion such as tricuspid regurgitation.
Radiation to the axilla is typical of mitral regurgitation, not aortic stenosis.

questions.stem: Adam, 74, has exertional breathlessness, chest tightness and syncope, with orthopnoea and PND. His echo shows a calcified trileaflet aortic valve, peak velocity 4.6 m/s, mean gradient 52 mmHg, AVA 0.7 cm² and LVEF 60%. He asks how it will be fixed. What is the definitive management?
options: Optimise antihypertensives and diuretics, then repeat the echo in 6 months
Heart team assessment for aortic valve replacement (TAVI or SAVR) with a tissue valve
Balloon aortic valvuloplasty as the definitive treatment of the stenosis
Surgical aortic valve replacement with a mechanical valve and lifelong warfarin
questions.why: Severe aortic stenosis with symptoms is a Class I indication for valve replacement, because without it the outlook is poor. At 74 the heart team weighs TAVI against SAVR, and a bioprosthetic (tissue) valve is preferred.
notes: Surveillance echo suits asymptomatic disease. Once severe aortic stenosis causes symptoms, medical therapy does not change survival.
Balloon valvuloplasty gives only short-lived benefit and restenosis is early, so it is used as a bridge or palliation, not as definitive treatment.
At 74 a tissue valve is preferred, because a mechanical valve needs lifelong warfarin and carries a higher bleeding risk in older patients.

questions.stem: Adam, 74, has severe calcific aortic stenosis. Twice in recent months, walking uphill, he became dizzy and briefly blacked out, then recovered at once. His ECG shows sinus rhythm with no heart block. What is the main mechanism of his exertional syncope?
options: Fixed outflow obstruction stops cardiac output rising as exercising muscle vasodilates
An exercise-triggered vagal surge causing bradycardia and venous pooling
Calcific emboli from the valve briefly blocking cerebral arteries
Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation from left atrial stretch reducing ventricular filling
questions.why: On exertion, resistance in the exercising muscles falls. The stenosed valve fixes stroke volume, so cardiac output cannot rise to match, blood pressure falls and cerebral perfusion drops.
notes: A vasovagal faint usually follows a trigger such as standing or pain and comes with a prodrome. It is not typically brought on by exertion in a patient with a fixed obstruction.
Emboli cause focal deficits that last as long as the TIA or stroke, not a global blackout with instant recovery on exertion.
He is in sinus rhythm with no palpitations. AF would also not explain a blackout brought on reliably by exertion.

questions.stem: Adam, 74, is told his narrowed aortic valve may be replaced 'through a tube from the groin' (transfemoral TAVI). A student is asked to palpate the femoral pulse that would be used for access. Where is the common femoral artery best palpated?
options: At the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, above the deep inguinal ring
Just lateral to the pubic tubercle, at the superficial inguinal ring
Medial to the femoral vein, deep to the lacunar ligament
At the mid-inguinal point, midway between ASIS and pubic symphysis
questions.why: The common femoral artery is felt at the mid-inguinal point, halfway between the ASIS and the pubic symphysis, just below the inguinal ligament. Order from lateral to medial: nerve, artery, vein, then the empty space and lymphatics (NAVEL).
notes: The midpoint of the inguinal ligament (halfway from ASIS to pubic tubercle) marks the deep inguinal ring. It lies slightly lateral to the artery.
The superficial inguinal ring, beside the pubic tubercle, is where the spermatic cord leaves the canal, not where the artery runs.
The artery lies lateral to the femoral vein. The space medial to the vein, near the lacunar ligament, is the femoral canal.
